latin.720: §. VI. Interim pro admittenda Impiorum Manducatione Orali Corporis Christi, tria admodum, præter jam tum subversa, & unum Biblicum, consequentia perquam non biblica laborans, adferri in medium consuevêre, quorum primum, à Natura Sacramentorum; Alterum, à Natura dati & crucifixi corporis Christi; Tertium à Concessione Reformatorum semel facta, videri cupiunt desumta; Quibus Quartum Professoris Wittenberg. accedit, petitum ab usu singulari fructuque quem hypothesis de Impiorum Manducatione Corporis Christi Orali, præstet, & à quo etiam Necessitatem Dogmatis ac Fundamentalitatem arcessit.
latin.721: BIBLICUM, in dicto Apostolico 1. Cor. 11. vers. 28. 29. se fundans, ita infert: Quicunque Communicantium, rei fiunt corporis Christi, illi manducant corpus Christi, si non spiritualiter, saltem oraliter, Impii &c. Ergo. Resp. Quam insulsa sit Major, rerum Sacrarum abusus fere quicunque ostendit, quô DEI, Christi, hujusque corporis & sanguinis, rei fiunt homines, Eucharistiam licet haud accedentes. Ab ipso Spiritu S. corporis & sanguinis Christi rei habentur ipsi etiam Apostatae, totum tamen Christianismum, nedum Sacramenta, abominati: Perhibentur enim crucifigere Christum & filium DEI ad ignominiam exponere Hebr. 6, 4. 5. 6. & Cap. 10. filium DEI conculcare & sanguinem fœderis profanum ducere, & Spiritum S. contumelia afficere. Quodsi ergo Apostatae rei fiunt corporis & sanguinis Christi, sacramentum deserendo, qui non rei fieri poterunt eorundem, Impii Christiani, Sacramento abutendo, i. e. manducando Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi, non rem Sacramenti, quâ se privant ipsos, etiam Sacramenti abusu.
latin.722: Connectitur proximè cum Biblico Argumento, ALTERUM illud, quod ad Naturam Sacramenti provocat, cujus integritatem sibi non constare opinatur, si Manducatio Corporis Christi Oralis, alicubi, h. e. in impiis, deficiat. Resp. (a) Indirectè: Sic nec constabit Sacramento integritas, si Manducatio spiritualis corporis Christi alicubi deficiat, quam in impiis deficere in confesso est. (b) Directè: Ad Sacramenti integritatem non pertinet, integrum accipi, sed sufficit, integrum offerri: Distinguendum itaque denuo inter Oblationem, & Receptionem. Ad hanc, ab illa, non valet consequentia: Omne enim receptivum recipit, non ad modum imprimentis, sed ad modum receptivitatis suæ.
latin.723: Institeris: Ita Sacramenta ab humana qualitate & actione eóque voluntate & arbitrio suspendi: Huc respiciunt quæ Clariss. Wittebergensis urget: Sacramentum hoc non fundari in hominum sanctitate, sed ipso Dei Verbo, quod nulla hominum incredulitate irritum reddi potest. Et quemadmodum nullus vel Sanctus in terris, vel Angelus in cælis, facere potest, ut Panis & Vinum sint C. & S. Christi; ita nemo illud Sacramentum mutare potest, ne sit Christi C. & S. etiamsi eodem abutatur. Christus enim non dixit: si credideritis, aut digni fueritis, tum in S. C. corpus & S. meum præsentia habebitis: Sed ait simpliciter: Edite, bibite: hoc est corpus meum, hic est sanguis meus; scribit Lutherus noster in Catech. Maj. P. 555.
latin.724: Resp. (a) Indirectè: Idem dici posse ratione spiritualis Manducationis. (b) Directè: Sacramenta esse restricta & suspensa non Intrinsecè & Constitutivè, sed Extrinsecè, Effectivè & Objectivè. Esse restricta ad requisita hominis, sed talia, quæ opus Dei, non hominum sunt. Hinc negatur consequentia: Sacramenta non operantur, nisi suppositâ fide hominis, Ergo Sacramentorum Operatio dependet ab Hominis arbitrio & opere. Quemadmodum non valet, vel juxta Lutheranos: Verbum DEI operatur Conversionem; Vel: Deus seu Spiritus S. convertit hominem eúmque donat fide, nisi rejiciat gratiam DEI, Ergo Conversio hominis dependet ab humano arbitrio: Nam quia illa ipsa potentia recipiendi & non recipiendi, in sensu composito, est opus DEI, non hominis, utpote, per gratiam prævenientem, cum annunciatione verbi divini, donata, Conversio quidem restringitur ad Requisitum in homine, sed ad tale, quod non homo, sed virtus & potentia DEI, operantur, ut non ab homine, sed DEO proficiscatur. Hoc pacto aërem quoque feriunt omnia, à Clariss. Viro, tam ex se, quam ex Luthero allata.
latin.725: At verò TERTIO LOCO urgent: Corpus Christi crucifixum datumque pro omnibus esse, Ergo ab omnibus, etiam indignis, manducari. Resp. (1) Indirectè, Ergo etiam à Judæis, Mahumedanis & Ethnicis? (2) Directè, distinguendo, ex communi hypothesi, inter Acquisitionem & Applicationem: A latitudine Acquisitionis, per Redemtionem factæ, ad Applicationis eandem latitudinem, non valet Consequentia.
latin.726: Denique QUARTO obtendunt: A Reformatis Impiorum Oralem corporis Christi Manducationem concessam olim esse, in Formula nempe Concordiæ Wittebergensis Anno 1536. sancitæ, & à Reformatorum pluribus subscripta, apud Chytræum, Histor. Aug. Confess. pag. 680. quin Helvetiis approbatæ, fatente Crocio in Comment. August. Conf. pag. 100. & 107.
latin.727: Respond. Reformatos, ad mentem Patrum Ecclesiæ antiquiorum, inter Sacramentum, & rem Sacramenti, item, Exhibitionem, & Receptionem, distinxisse, & prioris, non posterioris Manducationem veram & Receptionem Indignis addixisse. Ita enim verba Concordiæ habent: Sicut Paulus dicit, etiam Indignos SACRAMENTUM manducare, ita sentiunt etiam Concordiam ineuntes, indignis verè exhiberi Corpus & Sanguinem Christi & indignos VERE ACCIPERE, cùm institutio & MANDATUM (etiam de explorando se ipso) Christi Domini servantur. Sed tales accipiunt ad judicium, sicut Paulus inquit, quia abutuntur SACRAMENTO, cùm sine vera pœnitentia & fide accipiant. Ideo enim institutum est, ut testetur, Gratiam & beneficia Christi sumentibus applicari & verè Corpori Christi inserí & sanguine ejus ablui eos, qui pœnitentiam verè agunt & fide in Christum se consolantur. Confirmat idem declaratio Helvetiorum, etiam Crocio recensita, cit. loc. pag. 110. & Luthero approbata: ibid. p. 111.

pass_a.720: §. VI. Meanwhile, for admitting Oral Eating of Christ’s Body by the Impious, three arguments in particular — besides those already then overthrown — and one Biblical, laboring under a thoroughly unbiblical consequence, have customarily been brought forward, of which the first they wish to seem drawn from the Nature of the Sacraments; the Second from the Nature of Christ’s given and crucified body; the Third from a Concession once made by the Reformed; to which a Fourth of the Wittenberg Professor is added, sought from the singular use and fruit which the hypothesis of Oral Eating of Christ’s Body by the Impious is to furnish, and from which he also fetches the Necessity and Fundamentality of the Dogma.
pass_a.721: The BIBLICAL, founding itself on the Apostolic saying 1 Cor. 11:28–29, so infers: Whoever of the Communicants become guilty of Christ’s body, those eat Christ’s body — if not spiritually, at least orally — the Impious &c. Therefore. Reply: How insipid the Major is, almost every abuse of Sacred things shows — by which men become guilty of GOD, of Christ, and of his body and blood, though not approaching the Eucharist. By the Holy Spirit Himself even Apostates are held guilty of Christ’s body and blood, though they have abominated all Christianity, much less the Sacraments: For they are said to crucify Christ and expose the Son of GOD to shame (Heb 6:4–6) and (ch. 10) to trample the Son of GOD and count the blood of the covenant common and insult the Holy Spirit. If therefore Apostates become guilty of Christ’s body and blood by deserting the sacrament, how will not Impious Christians become guilty of the same by abusing the Sacrament — i.e. by eating the Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, not the Thing of the Sacrament, of which they deprive themselves even by abusing the Sacrament.
pass_a.722: Next connected with the Biblical Argument is that SECOND which appeals to the Nature of the Sacrament, whose integrity it thinks does not stand for itself if Oral Eating of Christ’s Body fails somewhere — i.e. in the Impious. Reply (a) Indirectly: Thus neither will integrity stand for the Sacrament if spiritual Eating of Christ’s body fails somewhere, which is confessed to fail in the Impious. (b) Directly: To the Sacrament’s integrity it does not pertain that the whole be received, but it suffices that the whole be offered: Therefore again Oblation and Reception must be distinguished. From the former to the latter the consequence does not hold: For every receptive thing receives not after the mode of the impressing, but after the mode of its own receptivity.
pass_a.723: You will press: Thus Sacraments are suspended from human quality and action and so from will and arbitrium: Here look what the most distinguished Wittenberger urges: This Sacrament is not founded in men’s holiness but in God’s own Word, which no men’s unbelief can render void. And as no Saint on earth or Angel in heaven can make Bread and Wine be C. & B. of Christ, so no one can change that Sacrament so that it not be Christ’s C. & B. even if he abuse the same. For Christ did not say: if you have believed, or been worthy, then in the H.S. you will have my body & B. present: But he says simply: Eat, drink: this is my body, this is my blood; our Luther writes in the Major Catechism p. 555.
pass_a.724: Reply (a) Indirectly: The same can be said by reason of spiritual Eating. (b) Directly: Sacraments are restricted and suspended not Intrinsically and Constitutively, but Extrinsically, Effectively and Objectively. They are restricted to requisites of man, but such as are God’s work, not men’s. Hence the consequence is denied: Sacraments do not operate unless man’s faith is supposed, Therefore the Sacraments’ Operation depends on Man’s arbitrium and work. Just as it does not hold, even on Lutheran terms: The Word of GOD works Conversion; Or: God or the Holy Spirit converts man and gifts him with faith unless he reject GOD’s grace, Therefore man’s Conversion depends on human arbitrium — for because that very power of receiving and not receiving, in the composed sense, is GOD’s work, not man’s, namely gifted by preventing grace with the announcing of the divine word, Conversion is indeed restricted to a Requisite in man, but to such as not man but GOD’s virtue and power work, so that it proceeds not from man but from GOD. In this way all that the most distinguished Man brought, both from himself and from Luther, also beat the air.
pass_a.725: But in the THIRD PLACE they urge: Christ’s Body was crucified and given for all, Therefore it is eaten by all, even the unworthy. Reply (1) Indirectly: Therefore also by Jews, Muslims, and Pagans? (2) Directly, distinguishing, on the common hypothesis, between Acquisition and Application: From the breadth of Acquisition made by Redemption to the same breadth of Application the Consequence does not hold.
pass_a.726: Finally FOURTH they put forward: that Oral Eating of Christ’s body by the Impious was once conceded by the Reformed, namely in the Formula of the Wittenberg Concord sanctioned in the Year 1536 and subscribed by many of the Reformed, in Chytraeus, History of the Augsburg Confession p. 680 — nay approved by the Swiss, Crocius confessing in Comment. on the Augustan Conf. pp. 100 & 107.
pass_a.727: Reply: The Reformed, after the mind of the older Fathers of the Church, distinguished between Sacrament and Thing of the Sacrament, likewise Exhibition and Reception, and assigned to the Unworthy true Eating and Reception of the former, not of the latter. For so the Concord’s words hold: As Paul says even the Unworthy eat the SACRAMENT, so also those entering the Concord sense that to the unworthy Body & Blood of Christ are truly exhibited and the unworthy TRULY RECEIVE, when the institution & MANDATE of Christ the Lord (also about examining oneself) are kept. But such receive unto judgment, as Paul says, because they abuse the SACRAMENT when they receive without true repentance and faith. For therefore it was instituted, to testify that Grace and Christ’s benefits are applied to those taking and that they are truly inserted into Christ’s Body and washed by his blood who truly repent and console themselves by faith in Christ. The Helvetians’ declaration confirms the same, also reviewed by Crocius, cited place p. 110, and approved by Luther: ibid. p. 111.

720: §.VI: for admitting Oral eating of Christ’s body by the Impious, three stock presses remain (plus one biblical) after the earlier ones fell.
From sacrament-nature; from the given/crucified body; from a Reformed concession; and a fourth Wittenberg press from the dogma’s supposed fruit, necessity, and fundamentality.
721: Biblical press (1 Cor 11:28–29): whoever becomes guilty of the body eats it — if not spiritually, then at least orally — so the Impious eat. Therefore.

Reply: the major is thin — men become guilty of God and of Christ’s body and blood by many abuses without approaching the Eucharist. Apostates are guilty while deserting the sacrament (Heb 6; 10); Impious Christians can be guilty by abusing the sacrament (eating the sign, not the Thing).
722: Second press: if Oral eating fails in the Impious, the sacrament’s integrity fails.
Reply: spiritual eating also fails in them, by confession; and integrity needs the whole offered, not the whole received — Oblation ≠ Reception; the receiver takes after its own receptivity.
723: Press further: then sacraments hang on human will. The Wittenberger cites Luther’s Major Catechism (p.555): the sacrament rests on God’s Word, not human holiness; no unbelief voids it; no saint or angel can make bread and wine not be Christ’s body and blood even under abuse.
Christ did not say “if you believe or are worthy”; he said simply Eat, drink: this is my body, this is my blood.
724: Reply: the same could be said of spiritual eating. Sacraments are restricted not constitutively but extrinsically — to requisites that are God’s work, not man’s arbitrium.

“No faith, no operation ⇒ depends on human will” fails the same way Lutheran conversion talk fails: the power to receive or not is itself God’s preventing gift with the word. So the Wittenberg/Luther citations beat the air.
725: Third press: Christ’s body was given and crucified for all, therefore eaten by all, even the unworthy.
Indirectly: then also by Jews, Muslims, and pagans? Directly: Acquisition by redemption is not the same breadth as Application.
726: Fourth press: the Reformed once conceded Impious Oral eating in the Wittenberg Concord of 1536 (Chytraeus; Swiss approval per Crocius).
727: Reply: after the older Fathers, the Reformed distinguished sacrament vs Thing, exhibition vs reception — and gave the unworthy the former, not the latter.

Concord itself: the unworthy truly receive the SACRAMENT unto judgment when they abuse it without repentance and faith; the institution testifies grace to true penitents. Helvetian declaration (and Luther’s approval) confirms. Stop §.VI before §.VII.
